 — Conflicting opinions exist on whether melting sea ice contributes to sea level rise due to differing assumptions about salinity and density

There are two main, mutually exclusive positions in the evidence. The dominant view (d1, d3, d4, d5, d9, d10, d12, d13, d14) is that melting sea ice does not raise sea level because floating ice displaces its own volume; this is the standard Archimedes’-principle explanation. A minority but explicit counter-position (d2, d6, d7) argues that when freshwater sea ice melts in saltwater, the resulting freshwater has a larger volume than the displaced saltwater, producing a small but non-zero rise (~2.6% or ~4 cm). These two positions are mutually exclusive within the same physical scope and are presented as genuine, competing research outcomes.

The final answer below states both positions neutrally and attributes them to the cited sources.

Melting sea ice contributes to sea level rise only under specific assumptions about salinity and density, while the conventional view is that it does not. The majority of sources explain that because sea ice is already floating, its meltwater displaces a volume of ocean water equal to the volume it will add when melted, so sea level does not change [d1,d3,d4,d5,d9,d10,d12,d13,d14]. In contrast, a minority of sources argue that when freshwater sea ice melts in denser saltwater, the freshwater produced has a slightly larger volume than the saltwater it displaced, leading to a small rise in sea level of about 2.6% (roughly 4 centimeters) [d2,d6,d7].
